As you fall toward a black hole, the universe starts looking very strange.
Its gravity bends light, so the stars behind it smear into glowing arcs and rings.
You can even see the same star twice.
Closer in, the black shadow swells to fill your view, and starlight piles up in a thin bright ring at its edge.
But what happens next depends on its size.
A small black hole, a few times the Sun's mass, pulls on your feet much harder than your head.
You'd be stretched like spaghetti and torn apart before you even reach the edge.
A giant one, like the monster at the center of our galaxy, is much gentler.
You'd cross the event horizon in one piece, without feeling anything special.
But now every path leads inward. Not even light can get out.
And a friend watching from far away would see you slow down, freeze at the edge, and fade into red.
